intro: A brain you can explore from two sides. Outside, tap the lobes, the motor and touch strips, and the language areas; inside, with the brain cut down the middle, find the corpus callosum, the thalamus and hypothalamus, the hippocampus and amygdala, and the brainstem. Press “If it is damaged” to see what changes when a region is hurt, light up a task as an fMRI scan would, and run the classic split-brain test: flash a word to one side and see which hemisphere gets it, whether the patient can say it, and which hand can find it.
howItWorksTitle: About the drawing and the cases
howItWorks:
The brain is a simplified illustration of an adult human brain: the outside view is the left hemisphere seen from the left, and the inside view is the inner surface of the right hemisphere after the brain is cut down the middle (both with the front on the left). Deep structures that cannot be seen from either surface (the hippocampus, amygdala and reward center) are drawn dashed, as if seen through the tissue. Area borders are approximate and vary between people.

Language is drawn in the left hemisphere, as it is for most people. The hemispheres specialize, but everyone uses both: there are no left-brained or right-brained people. Named cases are real and cited (Phineas Gage, H.M., S.M., Olds and Milner, Sperry and Gazzaniga); the other patients in the drills are invented for practice.
